title: Dotsero Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Dotsero wells have a 60-foot median depth, but fractured bedrock can make drilling cost $9,900-$18,000 for a finished well.
h1: Wells and Well Costs in Dotsero, Colorado
intro_html:
If you are buying land near Dotsero, the local well records point to relatively shallow wells overall, but not uniform drilling conditions. Among 131 permitted wells within five miles, the median reported depth is 60 feet. The middle half runs from 45 to 101 feet, while the deepest record reaches 500 feet.

Most permits identify an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer rather than a consistently mapped shallow water-bearing layer. That distinction matters when pricing a new well. A nearby permit is useful evidence, but it does not guarantee the same depth, water level, or production on your lot.

sections.heading: Dotsero well depths are usually shallow, with bedrock exceptions
sections.html:
Dotsero’s depth records lean shallow: 73% of wells are under 100 feet, 18% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 8% are between 300 and 600 feet. No recorded wells are 600 feet or deeper. The median is 60 feet, and the middle half of reported depths is 45 to 101 feet.

That spread is important for a drilling bid. A contractor may encounter productive rock near the local median, but the deepest record shows that a lot can behave very differently from its neighbors. Of 131 permitted wells, 71 report a total depth and 51 are recorded as constructed, so the statistics describe the available records rather than every possible well condition.

Permits name fractured bedrock on 126 wells and alluvial aquifer conditions on only three. Granite and gneiss can change quickly across short distances, so access, casing, grout, and final pump design still need site-specific review.

sections.heading: Most Dotsero yield records are strong, but test the actual lot
sections.html:
Reported production is favorable in this local record. The median yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half runs from 15.0 to 65.0 gallons per minute. Eighty percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Seventeen percent are in the 5-to-15 range, and 3% are in the 1-to-5 range. None of the reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

Only 30 wells report a pump yield, so do not treat the percentages as a guarantee for an untested parcel. Yield is also different from storage and pressure. A driller’s test, pump setting, storage tank, and household demand all affect how comfortably a well serves a home. Ask for the well construction report and pumping information before relying on a neighbor’s result.

sections.heading: Dotsero water levels are shallow in the available records
sections.html:
The 12 wells reporting a static water level show a median depth to water of 18 feet. The middle half is 14 to 28 feet. That suggests water is relatively near the surface in the wells with measurements, which can simplify pumping compared with a much deeper static level.

There is not enough information here to claim that the water table is falling or rising over time. The permit counts by decade show activity, not a water-level trend: records range from two permits in the 1960s to 36 in the 2000s, with the newest permit issued in 2025. A buyer should request the actual static-level measurements, well test, and seasonal information for the specific property.

Because most permits identify fractured bedrock, nearby water levels may not represent a single continuous shallow aquifer. Local fractures, elevation, and surface drainage can matter more than distance alone.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long use and several active drillers
sections.html:
Dotsero’s permit history extends from the 1960s through a newest permit year of 2025. The records include two permits from the 1960s, five from the 1970s, 16 from the 1980s, 18 from the 1990s, 36 from the 2000s, 19 from the 2010s, and 11 from the 2020s. Domestic or household use accounts for 50% of the listed use mix. Irrigation accounts for 15%, stock for 7%, and monitoring for 18%.

The most common driller names in the records are Shelton Drilling Corporation, associated with Shelton, Wayne, with 26 wells; Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation, associated with Shelton, Joe Wayne, with eight; and Collins Drilling Co, associated with Collins, F. E. “Bodie,” with seven.

These names can help you find local construction history, but they do not replace a current site evaluation or bid.

sections.heading: A Dotsero well at the median depth may cost $9,900-$18,000 finished
sections.html:
Dotsero is fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The drilling model uses a rate of $65-$100 per foot. At the local median depth of 60 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $3,900-$6,000.

A finished well is more than the hole. With a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, the modeled total at that depth is about $9,900-$18,000. The lower end is not a promise, because mobilization, difficult rock, casing, grout, access, water testing, and site-specific electrical work can change the bid.

The deepest recorded well is 500 feet, illustrating why a per-foot allowance matters. Ask each driller what is included, how additional footage is handled, and what happens if the hole is dry or produces less water than expected. Compare bids on the same scope rather than on drilling price alone.

sections.heading: Check PFAS, mine features, septic layout, and dry-hole exposure
sections.html:
Environmental review deserves attention around Dotsero. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 10 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 13 historic mine features. There are no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the supplied records. Those findings do not establish contamination on a particular parcel, but they are reasons to check maps, land history, and current water-quality results.

Low yield is not prominent in the reported sample, yet only 30 wells list a pump yield and fractured rock remains unpredictable. A dry hole or weak production should be addressed in the drilling contract. Confirm casing, grout, wellhead protection, and a certified water test.

Before building, confirm the septic reserve area, setbacks, driveway access, electrical route, and water-rights requirements. A domestic exempt well may support household use, but irrigation or other uses can require separate review, and an augmentation plan may be relevant in an over-appropriated basin.

sections.heading: Use nearby records, then verify the Dotsero parcel itself
sections.html:
Start with the actual permit file for the lot, then compare it with nearby records in Dotsero and the surrounding area. Gypsum is about five miles away, Eagle about 12 miles, and No Name about 14 miles. Cattle Creek, El Jebel, and Carbonate are each about 17 miles away, but records farther from the parcel should be treated as background rather than a direct prediction.

For a purchase, make the contract contingent on reviewing the permit, construction report, water test, pump information, and legal well use. If the parcel has no well, get a driller’s site opinion and a written allowance for extra footage and completion work. If you plan a home, coordinate the well, septic system, driveway, trenching, and power route before finalizing the building site.

That process is more reliable than assuming the 60-foot median or 15.0-gallon-per-minute median will apply to your ground.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Dotsero?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Dotsero is 60 feet. The middle half of reported depths is 45 to 101 feet, and 73% are under 100 feet. The deepest record reaches 500 feet. Most permits identify fractured bedrock, so a nearby shallow well does not guarantee the same depth on another lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Dotsero?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate in Dotsero is $65-$100 per foot. At the 60-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $3,900-$6,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $9,900-$18,000. Fractured granite and gneiss can require additional footage or completion work.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Dotsero?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 15.0 to 65.0 gallons per minute. Eighty percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 30 wells report a pump yield, however, so a buyer should obtain the specific well test rather than rely only on area statistics.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Dotsero?
faq.a: The supplied records identify 10 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 13 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those area findings do not determine a parcel’s water quality. Test the well for common drinking-water concerns and review nearby land and mine history before occupying a home.

faq.q: Can I build a home on a well in Dotsero?
faq.a: A buildable lot needs more than a nearby well permit. Confirm the well’s permitted use, production, water quality, septic layout, access, power, and building setbacks. Domestic household use makes up 50% of the local use mix. Irrigation is 15%, and other uses may require additional water-rights review or an augmentation plan.
